Sergei Korolev. Soviet chief rocket designer who led the Soviet space program from Sputnik through the Vostok manned missions. Though his name was withheld from the public during his lifetime for security reasons, Korolev was the architect of the Soviet space triumph and a visionary planner who envisioned the first lunar landing.

He was the chief designer of the R-7 rocket, the first intercontinental ballistic missile, which was adapted to launch Sputnik 1 in nineteen fifty-seven. This first artificial satellite shocked the West into the Space Race. Korolev designed the Vostok spacecraft and oversaw the first crewed spaceflight: Yuri Gagarin on April 12, nineteen sixty-one. This was a propaganda victory that established Soviet superiority in space.

Korolev planned an ambitious Soviet lunar program, including the N1 rocket intended as a Soviet answer to the Saturn V. The N1 failed repeatedly, and the Soviet Union never reached the moon. He worked in secrecy under the Soviet system. His name was classified and not publicly revealed until after his death, making him an unknown giant to the West while he shaped history.

Korolev endured imprisonment during Stalin's purges between nineteen thirty-eight and nineteen forty-four and survived wartime hardship. Yet he rebuilt Soviet rocket design from captured German V-2s and indigenous innovation. He died suddenly in January nineteen sixty-six during surgery, at age fifty-nine, depriving the Soviet program of his leadership during its final push for the moon.
